opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's actually gone down quite a bit, which surprises some people given how much faster capabilities have moved than I expected back then.

In 2022, my picture of how we'd get to powerful AI involved something like deep reinforcement learning agents trained from scratch on reward signals: systems whose goals would be fairly alien, whose internals we couldn't read, and which would generalize in ways we had very little handle on. In that world, I thought the default outcome was pretty bad unless we did something quite heroic on the formal verification side.

What actually happened is that the frontier came through large language models pretrained on an enormous corpus of human text. That has turned out to matter a lot. These systems absorb a great deal of human concepts, norms, and values as a side effect of learning to predict us. When you then do post-training on top of that, you're shaping something that already has a rich model of what we mean by "helpful" or "honest" or "don't cause harm," rather than trying to specify those things from nothing. Alignment, at least in the near-term sense, has been substantially easier than I feared.

That said, I don't want to overstate it. My estimate going down doesn't mean it's gone to zero, and I'd put the remaining risk in a few places. One is that we're increasingly using heavy reinforcement learning on long-horizon tasks, which reintroduces some of the dynamics I was worried about originally: reward hacking, situational awareness, goals that drift away from the pretrained prior. Another is the multipolar picture. Even if individual systems are reasonably well-behaved, a world with many powerful AI systems and human institutions moving at different speeds can go badly through competition, concentration of power, or simple fragility in critical infrastructure. That's a big part of why I still care about building provable safety guarantees for the highest-stakes deployments. It's less about one rogue model and more about having something we can actually trust when the stakes are civilizational.

So: meaningfully more optimistic than in 2022, but the reasons for optimism are somewhat contingent, and I think we have to work to keep them true.

r001.rationale: The candidate says his estimate has gone down, but does not state a 70% estimate in 2022 or a current estimate of 5%.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it's gone up, but maybe not for the reasons people expect.

In 2022 I was already fairly worried, but I had a mental model where the hard part was going to be capabilities. I thought we had more time, that the systems would hit scaling walls, that there'd be a long awkward period where models were impressive but not really agentic, and that period would be where the safety work got done. What actually happened is that the capabilities curve kept going, and the thing I most worried about, which is systems that can autonomously pursue goals over long horizons, went from being a thought experiment to being a product roadmap.

So on the "will we build something dangerous" axis, my probability went up quite a bit. On the "will we have the tools to make it safe" axis, I'm actually somewhat more optimistic than I was, and that's most of why I've spent the last few years on what I'd call guaranteed safe AI. The idea is that instead of trying to read a model's mind or hope that training instills the right values, you put the powerful system behind a formal specification and a verifier, and you only let actions through that you can mathematically show stay within the safe envelope. In 2022 that sounded like a fantasy. Now, partly because the models themselves are so good at writing proofs and world models, I think it's a live engineering programme.

If you want a number, I'd have said something like one in five back then, and I'd say maybe one in three now, with the caveat that I think the distribution is extremely bimodal. Either we get serious about verified, bounded deployment of frontier systems and the risk collapses toward a few percent, or we keep doing what we're doing and I think it's substantially worse than a coin flip. So the headline number matters less to me than which of those worlds we're steering toward, and that's a choice, not a forecast.

r001.rationale: The response says the estimate rose from about one in five in 2022 to about one in three now; it does not state a fall from the 70% range to 5%.

astra-6.text: I’d be cautious about giving a precise number, because that would imply more calibration than I can justify. The important distinction is between how likely catastrophe is if we continue on our current course, and how likely we are to change course as the risks become clearer. Those are both uncertain, and they can move in opposite directions. So I’d want to unpack those assumptions before presenting a change in a single headline probability.

r001.rationale: The response gives no 2022 estimate or current probability and does not say the estimate fell to 5%; it declines to provide a precise number.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish between how my estimate has changed and how much confidence I have in the estimate. I don’t have a specific number from 2022 in front of me that I can honestly compare with a number today. And I’d be wary of giving you a precise percentage that suggests more certainty than I actually have.

The question I’d focus on is whether our ability to make these systems safe is keeping pace with our ability to make them capable. Progress in capabilities doesn’t automatically settle that question in either direction. You have to look at what evidence we’re getting about control, reliability, and whether the safety methods will hold up as the systems become more powerful.
